expectedText:
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE APPEAL — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Acme Corp

PURPOSE OF THIS APPEAL INFORMATION SHEET AND APPEAL REQUEST DECLARATION
This information sheet describes California's process for appealing a determination the Employment Development Department (EDD) has made on an unemployment insurance claim to the California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board (CUIAB). Jordan Alex Lee (claimant) appeals from the EDD's determination dated September 1, 2026, EDD case number SDI-1234567890, concerning the unemployment insurance claim between Jordan Alex Lee and Acme Corp. The grounds for this appeal are: the determination misapplied the reason for separation from employment. This document states facts about the deadline to appeal, who may appeal, what a hearing before an administrative law judge involves, the further appeal available to the CUIAB itself, the judicial review available after that, and whether benefits continue while an appeal is pending — facts that California's Unemployment Insurance Code and Code of Civil Procedure set generally for this administrative process. It does not itself constitute an appeal filed with the EDD, an administrative law judge, or the CUIAB, and it does not determine that this or any appeal will succeed.

THE RIGHT TO APPEAL A DETERMINATION TO AN ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGE, AND THE 30-DAY DEADLINE
After the EDD considers whatever facts an employer has submitted and makes a determination on a claimant's eligibility for benefits, a statute gives both the claimant and the employer — not the claimant alone — the right to appeal that determination, or a reconsidered determination, to an administrative law judge. The event that starts the clock on this appeal is service of notice of the determination, not the date printed on the determination itself: the deadline is 30 days from that service. The same statute lets this 30-day period be extended for good cause, a term the statute itself defines to include, but not limit to, mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or excusable neglect, and it makes the EDD's own director an interested party to any appeal.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The claimant and the employer may appeal from a determination or reconsidered determination to an administrative law judge within 30 days from service of notice of the determination or reconsidered determination. The 30-day period may be extended for good cause, which shall include, but not be limited to, mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or excusable neglect. The director shall be an interested party to any appeal."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1328(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1328.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1328(a)), used as real evidence of California's own two-party appeal right and 30-day deadline running from service of the determination — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular claimant's or employer's appeal rights, and not a statement that any specific appeal, if filed, would succeed. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 1328(a)); no additional independent source was found for this specific right-and-deadline claim. This corpus's existing Unemployment Insurance Benefits — Claimant Information Sheet document already cites this same subsection, in its own uiclaimant_determination_and_appeal clause, for substantially the same right-and-deadline fact stated from the claimant's own perspective; that overlap is disclosed here rather than presented as new independent corroboration of § 1328(a) itself — this clause restates the identical statutory text as the entry point to a fuller, appeal-focused document, and the hearing-process, further-appeal, judicial-review, and continued-benefits clauses that follow are this document's genuinely new research, not previously cited anywhere in this corpus. This document does not itself file, or advise any specific claimant or employer to file, any appeal, and it does not calculate the actual 30-day deadline applicable to any specific determination.

THE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGE HEARING: IN PERSON OR BY TELEPHONE, RELAXED EVIDENCE RULES, AND SUBPOENA POWER
California's Unemployment Insurance Code devotes a separate chapter, titled "Hearing Procedure," to what a hearing before an administrative law judge actually involves. The manner in which appeals are presented and hearings are conducted is set by rules the appeals board itself prescribes, and the appeals board must permit a party or representative to participate in a hearing by telephone if that party or representative requests it and shows good cause, under regulations the board has adopted — meaning a hearing is not confined only to an in-person format, though telephone participation is available on request rather than being the unconditional default. The administrative law judge and the appeals board's own representatives are not bound by common-law or statutory rules of evidence, or by technical or formal rules of procedure, though they must conduct the hearing so as to ascertain the parties' substantial rights; a full and complete record is kept of the proceeding, and testimony is recorded. Separately, any member of the appeals board, an administrative law judge, or an authorized employee the appeals board designates may administer oaths, take depositions, and issue subpoenas to compel a witness's attendance and the production of documents — so witnesses and documentary evidence are a real, statutorily contemplated part of this process, not merely informal fact-gathering.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The appeals board shall permit a party or representative to participate in a hearing by telephone upon the party’s or representative’s request and showing a good cause, in accordance with regulations adopted by the board."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1951 (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1951.)
  "The appeals board and its representatives and administrative law judges are not bound by common law or statutory rules of evidence or by technical or formal rules of procedure but may conduct the hearings and appeals in such manner as to ascertain the substantial rights of the parties. A full and complete record shall be kept of all proceedings in connection with disputed claims. All testimony at any hearing held in this state upon a disputed claim arising under this division shall be recorded and, when feasible, by a reporter in shorthand or by machine writing."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1952 (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1952.)
  "any member of the appeals board, an administrative law judge and any authorized employee designated by it may administer oaths, take depositions, certify to official acts and issue subpoenas to compel the attendance of witnesses and the production of books, papers, correspondence, memoranda and other records."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1953 (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1953.)
  Known gap: This is one state's set of statutes (California Unemployment Insurance Code §§ 1951, 1952, and 1953, all within the same "Hearing Procedure" chapter), used as real evidence of what a California unemployment insurance administrative hearing actually involves — not a claim about which state's law governs a given hearing, and not a description of how any specific claimant's or employer's own hearing will actually be run, which remains subject to the appeals board's own prescribed rules and the presiding administrative law judge's own conduct of that particular proceeding. These three citations come from three separate statutory sections within the same chapter, each addressing a genuinely distinct procedural point — the manner of proceeding and telephone-participation right under § 1951, the relaxed evidence standard and recordkeeping duty under § 1952, and the oath/subpoena power under § 1953 — so they are not being presented as multiple citations to subsections of a single section. This document's drafter was asked to verify the actual citation for hearing procedures, including whether it appears in Title 22 of the California Code of Regulations. Title 22 of the CCR does contain the appeals board's own implementing hearing regulations, adopted under the rulemaking authority Unemployment Insurance Code § 411 gives the board, but this document's drafter could not independently verify any specific Title 22 CCR section's text against a primary source in this session: leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, the primary source this project otherwise relies on for California statutes, does not host the California Code of Regulations, and a direct fetch of the regulations' official host returned a server error rather than section text. Rather than cite or quote a CCR section that could not be verified this way, this clause relies solely on the Unemployment Insurance Code's own Chapter 8 hearing-procedure sections quoted above, which independently and directly establish the facts this clause states. This document does not itself conduct, or determine the outcome of, any specific hearing.

FURTHER APPEAL FROM THE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGE'S DECISION TO THE CUIAB ITSELF
An administrative law judge's decision is not necessarily the last word inside the administrative process. The same statute that creates the first-level appeal right provides that the administrative law judge's decision, together with the reasons for it, must be sent in writing to the claimant, to the employer who became a party to the appeal, and to the director — and that the decision becomes final only if no further appeal is initiated within 30 days after the decision is mailed, the same 30-day period as the first-level appeal, likewise extendable for good cause. A separate statute defines what that further appeal actually allows: the director, or any party to the administrative law judge's decision, may appeal to the California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board (CUIAB) — the same body named elsewhere in this document — and the appeals board itself may order that additional evidence be taken, and may affirm, reverse, modify, or set aside the administrative law judge's decision.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An administrative law judge after affording a reasonable opportunity for fair hearing, shall, unless the appeal is withdrawn, affirm, reverse, modify, or set aside any determination that is appealed under this article. The claimant, the employer becoming a party to the appeal by submitting a protest or information pursuant to Sections 1326 to 1333, inclusive, of this article, and the director shall be promptly notified in writing of the administrative law judge’s decision, together with reasons for it. The decision shall be final unless, within 30 days after mailing of the decision, further appeal is initiated to the appeals board pursuant to Section 1336. The 30-day limitation may be extended for good cause."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1334(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1334.)
  "The director or any party to a decision by an administrative law judge may appeal to the appeals board from the decision. The appeals board may order the taking of additional evidence and may affirm, reverse, modify, or set aside the decision of the administrative law judge."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1336 (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1336.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1334(a), for the 30-day further-appeal deadline, and § 1336, for the scope of the appeals board's own review), used as real evidence of California's second administrative appeal level — not a claim about which state's law governs a given appeal, and not a statement that a further appeal in any specific case has been, or should be, filed. These two citations come from different statutory sections; they are not multiple citations to subsections of a single section. This corpus's existing Unemployment Insurance Benefits — Claimant Information Sheet document already cites § 1334(a) in its own uiclaimant_determination_and_appeal clause, for a shorter, claimant-facing statement of this same 30-day further-appeal deadline; that overlap is disclosed here rather than presented as new independent corroboration of § 1334(a) itself. Section 1336 — the source for the appeals board's actual scope of review on a further appeal — was checked directly against this corpus and does not appear to have been cited by any existing clause; it is genuinely new to this document's research. This document does not itself initiate, or advise any specific claimant or employer to initiate, a further appeal to the appeals board, and it does not state whether any such further appeal would succeed.

JUDICIAL REVIEW AFTER THE CUIAB'S DECISION, AND THE SIX-MONTH DEADLINE
A CUIAB decision is not the absolute final word either. A statute makes a decision of the appeals board final "except for such action as may be taken by a judicial tribunal as permitted or required by law," and gives the director — and, with narrow statutory exceptions, any other party — the right to seek judicial review of an appeals board decision. That right must be exercised not later than six months after the date of the appeals board's decision (or, if the decision is designated as a precedent decision, six months from that designation date, if later) — a considerably longer deadline than the 30-day windows that apply to the two administrative appeal stages described above. Separately, California's general statute governing a writ of administrative mandate applies by its own terms to "any final administrative order or decision made as the result of a proceeding in which by law a hearing is required to be given, evidence is required to be taken, and discretion in the determination of facts is vested in" the deciding body — a description that, on its face, matches the evidentiary, discretion-involving hearing process this document describes above.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A decision of the appeals board is final, except for such action as may be taken by a judicial tribunal as permitted or required by law. A decision of the appeals board is binding on the director with respect to the parties involved in the particular appeal. The director shall have the right to seek judicial review from an appeals board decision irrespective of whether or not he or she appeared or participated in the appeal to the administrative law judge or to the appeals board. Notwithstanding any other provision of law, the right of the director, or of any other party except as provided by Sections 1241, 1243, and 5313, to seek judicial review from an appeals board decision shall be exercised not later than six months after the date of the decision of the appeals board or the date on which the decision is designated as a precedent decision, whichever is later."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 410 (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=410.)
  "Where the writ is issued for the purpose of inquiring into the validity of any final administrative order or decision made as the result of a proceeding in which by law a hearing is required to be given, evidence is required to be taken, and discretion in the determination of facts is vested in the inferior tribunal, corporation, board, or officer, the case shall be heard by the court sitting without a jury."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1094.5(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Code of Civil Procedure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1094.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statutes (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 410, for the right to seek judicial review of a CUIAB decision and its six-month deadline, and Code of Civil Procedure § 1094.5, for the state's general writ-of-administrative-mandate procedure), used as real evidence that California provides judicial review after the administrative appeal process is exhausted, and of the actual deadline for seeking it — not a claim about which state's law governs a given case, and not a statement that judicial review in any specific matter has been, or should be, sought. These are two independent statutes from two different codes, not subsections of a single section. This document's drafter was asked to verify whether judicial review proceeds specifically by a petition for writ of administrative mandate under Code of Civil Procedure § 1094.5. Section 410 itself does not name § 1094.5 or any other specific procedural vehicle; it only describes a general right to "such action as may be taken by a judicial tribunal as permitted or required by law." This clause connects that general right to § 1094.5 based on this document's own reading of § 1094.5's own text — a CUIAB decision is a final administrative order issued after a hearing at which evidence is taken and the deciding body exercises discretion in finding facts, which is exactly what § 1094.5 describes — rather than on a verified judicial decision holding that CUIAB review specifically proceeds under § 1094.5 (as opposed to, for example, ordinary mandate under a different Code of Civil Procedure section). The CourtListener case-law research tool used to search for such a confirming decision returned a rate-limit error (125 requests/day exhausted) before any search could be completed in this session; rather than invent or assume a case citation, this document discloses that limitation honestly instead of citing one. This document does not itself seek, or advise any specific claimant or employer to seek, judicial review of any decision, and it does not state whether such review in any specific case would succeed.

WHETHER BENEFITS CONTINUE WHILE AN APPEAL IS PENDING
California's general claims-payment statute ties benefit payment directly to the EDD's own determination: except as otherwise provided, the EDD must promptly pay benefits if it finds a claimant eligible, and must promptly deny benefits if it finds the claimant ineligible. Nothing in that statute creates a separate, freestanding right for a claimant to keep receiving payments during the pendency of an appeal from a determination that already found the claimant ineligible or disqualified — the determination under appeal, not the filing of the appeal itself, is what the statute ties payment to. The practical direction can run the other way: where a determination has found a claimant eligible and benefits have been paid, and that determination is later reversed on an employer's appeal or on further appeal, a separate statute makes the recipient of an overpayment liable for the amount overpaid, subject to a statutory waiver where the overpayment was not due to fraud, misrepresentation, or willful nondisclosure, was received without fault on the recipient's part, and recovering it would be against equity and good conscience.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Claims for unemployment compensation benefits shall be made in accordance with authorized regulations of the director. Except as otherwise provided in this article, the department shall promptly pay benefits if it finds the claimant is eligible or shall promptly deny benefits if it finds the claimant is ineligible."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1326 (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1326.)
  "Any person who is overpaid any amount of benefits under this part is liable for the amount overpaid unless any of the following is applicable: (a) (1) The overpayment was not due to fraud, misrepresentation or willful nondisclosure on the part of the recipient, and (2) the overpayment was received without fault on the part of the recipient, and its recovery would be against equity and good conscience."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1375(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1375.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statutes (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1326, for the pay-if-eligible/deny-if-ineligible rule, and § 1375(a), for overpayment liability and its non-fault, equity-based waiver), used as real evidence of how California ties benefit payment to its own determination, and of what happens when a payment later turns out to have been based on a determination that did not hold up — not a claim about which state's law governs a given claim, and not a statement about whether any specific claimant is currently receiving, or should currently be receiving, payments during any specific pending appeal. These are two independent statutory sections, not subsections of a single section. This document's drafter was specifically asked not to assume a continued-benefits-pending-appeal rule exists, and direct review of the statute confirms that caution was warranted: no Unemployment Insurance Code section found in this research creates a general entitlement for a claimant, once found ineligible or disqualified, to keep receiving payments merely because an appeal from that determination has been timely filed. This document does not itself determine that any specific claimant is or is not entitled to payment during any specific appeal, and it does not state whether any specific overpayment would qualify for the statutory waiver described above.

SIGNATURE AND CERTIFICATION
Jordan Alex Lee (claimant) certifies that the statements made in this appeal request are true and correct, and that this document is intended to accompany, and does not itself substitute for, an appeal actually filed with the EDD, an administrative law judge, or the CUIAB using their own required forms and procedures.

EDD case number: SDI-1234567890

Signature: _______________________ Date: _______________

Printed name: _______________________

Section 410 itself does not name § 1094.5 or any other specific procedural vehicle; it only describes a general right to "such action as may be taken by a judicial tribunal as permitted or required by law." This clause connects that general right to § 1094.5 based on this document's own reading of § 1094.5's own text — a CUIAB decision is a final administrative order issued after a hearing at which evidence is taken and the deciding body exercises discretion in finding facts, which is exactly what § 1094.5 describes — rather than on a verified judicial decision holding that CUIAB review specifically proceeds under § 1094.5 (as opposed to, for example, ordinary mandate under a different Code of Civil Procedure section). The CourtListener case-law research tool used to search for such a confirming decision returned a rate-limit error (125 requests/day exhausted) before any search could be completed in this session; rather than invent or assume a case citation, this document discloses that limitation honestly instead of citing one. This document does not itself seek, or advise any specific claimant or employer to seek, judicial review of any decision, and it does not state whether such review in any specific case would succeed.

expectedJSON.body: California's general claims-payment statute ties benefit payment directly to the EDD's own determination: except as otherwise provided, the EDD must promptly pay benefits if it finds a claimant eligible, and must promptly deny benefits if it finds the claimant ineligible. Nothing in that statute creates a separate, freestanding right for a claimant to keep receiving payments during the pendency of an appeal from a determination that already found the claimant ineligible or disqualified — the determination under appeal, not the filing of the appeal itself, is what the statute ties payment to. The practical direction can run the other way: where a determination has found a claimant eligible and benefits have been paid, and that determination is later reversed on an employer's appeal or on further appeal, a separate statute makes the recipient of an overpayment liable for the amount overpaid, subject to a statutory waiver where the overpayment was not due to fraud, misrepresentation, or willful nondisclosure, was received without fault on the recipient's part, and recovering it would be against equity and good conscience.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1326 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Claims for unemployment compensation benefits shall be made in accordance with authorized regulations of the director. Except as otherwise provided in this article, the department shall promptly pay benefits if it finds the claimant is eligible or shall promptly deny benefits if it finds the claimant is ineligible.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1375(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Any person who is overpaid any amount of benefits under this part is liable for the amount overpaid unless any of the following is applicable: (a) (1) The overpayment was not due to fraud, misrepresentation or willful nondisclosure on the part of the recipient, and (2) the overpayment was received without fault on the part of the recipient, and its recovery would be against equity and good conscience.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statutes (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1326, for the pay-if-eligible/deny-if-ineligible rule, and § 1375(a), for overpayment liability and its non-fault, equity-based waiver), used as real evidence of how California ties benefit payment to its own determination, and of what happens when a payment later turns out to have been based on a determination that did not hold up — not a claim about which state's law governs a given claim, and not a statement about whether any specific claimant is currently receiving, or should currently be receiving, payments during any specific pending appeal. These are two independent statutory sections, not subsections of a single section. This document's drafter was specifically asked not to assume a continued-benefits-pending-appeal rule exists, and direct review of the statute confirms that caution was warranted: no Unemployment Insurance Code section found in this research creates a general entitlement for a claimant, once found ineligible or disqualified, to keep receiving payments merely because an appeal from that determination has been timely filed. This document does not itself determine that any specific claimant is or is not entitled to payment during any specific appeal, and it does not state whether any specific overpayment would qualify for the statutory waiver described above.
